section: words as vectors: word2vec and glove
text: Before 2013 the usual input was a one-hot vector per word, in which every pair of words is equally far apart. word2vec learned a dense vector per word from raw text with a deliberately shallow model, so it could be trained on billions of words ( Mikolov et al.
label: core

section: words as vectors: word2vec and glove
text: 2013a ): Skip-gram predicts the words around a word from the word; CBOW (continuous bag of words) predicts a word from the average of its neighbours.
label: depth

section: words as vectors: word2vec and glove
text: The full softmax over a vocabulary of millions is too expensive, so the first paper used a hierarchical softmax (a Huffman tree, about log 2 V outputs per word) and the second replaced it with negative sampling ( Mikolov et al.
label: depth

section: words as vectors: word2vec and glove
text: 2013b ): push the true (word, context) pair together and k random words apart. log σ( v′ c · v w ) + Σ i =1.. k E n i ~ P n log σ(− v′ n i · v w ) v w , v′ c input vector of the word, output vector of a context word k negatives per pair: 5 to 20 for small corpora, 2 to 5 for large ones P n the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power, which beat both the plain unigram and the uniform distribution (§2.2); frequent words are also subsampled (§2.3) GloVe took the other route: count first, then fit ( Pennington, Socher and Manning 2014 ).
label: depth

section: words as vectors: word2vec and glove
text: Build the global word-by-word co-occurrence matrix X (pairs d words apart counted as 1/ d ), then fit vectors so that their dot product matches the log count, by weighted least squares: J = Σ i , j f ( X ij ) ( w i · w̃ j + b i + b̃ j − log X ij ) 2 , f ( x ) = min(1, ( x / x max ) α ) f down-weights rare pairs and caps frequent ones; the paper uses x max = 100, α = 3/4, AdaGrad, and the sum W + W̃ as the final vectors The two are closer than they look: skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorises the word-context pointwise mutual information matrix shifted by log k ( Levy and Goldberg 2014 ), so "predictive" (word2vec) against "count-based" (GloVe) is a difference of method more than of what is learned.
label: depth
key: pairs d words apart counted as 1/ d

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: Recurrent networks and backpropagation through time A recurrent network reads a sequence one element at a time and carries a hidden state forward ( Elman 1990 ): a t = f ( U x t + W a t −1 + b ), y t = g ( V a t ) a t the hidden state, the network's whole memory of the past U, W, V input, recurrent and output weights, the same at every step : the network has a fixed number of parameters whatever the sequence length f, g usually tanh for the state; softmax for a distribution over outputs It is trained by backpropagation through time (BPTT; Werbos 1990 ): unroll the network into one layer per time step, all sharing weights, run ordinary backpropagation, and add up the gradients each copy contributes to the shared weights.
label: core

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: Long sequences are usually cut into windows (truncated BPTT), which also caps how far back any gradient can reach.
label: core

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: The gradient from step t back to step k contains the product of Jacobians ∏ ∂ a j /∂ a j −1 = ∏ diag( f ′) W , one factor per step.
label: core

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio made the condition exact: if the largest eigenvalue of W (in absolute value) is below 1/γ, where γ bounds | f ′| (1 for tanh, 1/4 for the sigmoid), the long-term terms vanish exponentially; above it is necessary, not sufficient, for them to explode ( 2013 , §2.1).
label: core

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: Exploding gradients have a cheap fix, clipping the gradient's norm, which the same paper proposed; vanishing ones need a change of architecture.
label: core

section: recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
text: The difficulty itself was identified in Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis and by Bengio, Simard and Frasconi 1994 .
label: core

text: The LSTM, gate by gate The long short-term memory network gives each unit a memory cell C whose update is an addition, guarded by gates ( Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997 ).
label: core

text: The input x t and the previous hidden state h t −1 are concatenated and fed to four parallel layers; three of them are sigmoid gates , outputs between 0 and 1 that multiply a stream of information element by element.
label: core
key: fed to all four in parallel

text: Part Formula Role Forget gate f t = σ( W f [ h t −1 , x t ] + b f ) how much of the old cell C t −1 to keep Input gate i t = σ( W i [ h t −1 , x t ] + b i ) which units to write Candidate C̃ t = tanh( W C [ h t −1 , x t ] + b C ) what would be written Output gate o t = σ( W o [ h t −1 , x t ] + b o ) what part of the cell to expose Updates C t = f t ⊙ C t −1 + i t ⊙ C̃ t ; h t = o t ⊙ tanh( C t ) the cell is added to, not rewritten Why it works.
label: core
key: the cell is added to, not rewritten

text: Along the cell, ∂ C t /∂ C t −1 = diag( f t ) plus terms through the gates' dependence on h : no weight matrix and no squashing slope on the direct path, only the forget gate, which the network can hold near 1.
label: core
key: no weight matrix and no squashing slope

text: It is a skip connection through time, the same idea residual networks later used through depth.
label: core

text: It does not abolish vanishing gradients: the path through h still multiplies Jacobians, and a forget gate of 0.9 still shrinks the cell path by 0.9 50 ≈ 0.005 over 50 steps.
label: core

text: Setting the forget-gate bias to 1 or more at initialisation, so that the cell starts by remembering, is the standard recommendation ( Jozefowicz, Zaremba and Sutskever 2015 ) and is used in the model below.
label: core

text: Correction: the 1997 LSTM had no forget gate The original LSTM had input and output gates around a "constant error carrousel", a cell whose self-connection was fixed at 1.0 (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997, §3.2 and §4).
label: core

text: The forget gate, which lets the cell decay or reset, was added by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins 2000 , and "peephole" connections from the cell to the gates by Gers and Schmidhuber the same year.
label: core

text: The LSTM in every library today is the 2000 version, usually without peepholes ( Greff et al.

section: attention: let the decoder look back
text: Attention: let the decoder look back Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014, published at ICLR 2015) kept every encoder state h j (from a bidirectional RNN, so each state sees the whole sentence) and, at every output step i , let the decoder choose which to read: e ij = v ⊤ tanh( W s i −1 + U h j ), α ij = softmax j ( e ij ), c i = Σ j α ij h j s i−1 the decoder's state before writing word i e ij "alignment" score: how well source position j matches what the decoder needs now; a small network, so this is called additive attention c i a fresh context vector for every output word, fed to the decoder with the previous word The decoder now reads as many numbers as the source has states, so nothing has to be squeezed.
label: core

section: attention: let the decoder look back
text: In the paper's Table 1, trained on sentences up to 50 words, the attention model (RNNsearch-50) scored 26.75 BLEU against 17.82 for the same encoder-decoder without it (RNNencdec-50), and the attention model trained on sentences up to 30 words (21.50) beat the plain one trained up to 50.

text: What shipped in the Google Assistant in 2017 was Parallel WaveNet : a feed-forward student distilled from a trained WaveNet ("probability density distillation"), more than 20 times faster than real time, "deployed online by Google Assistant, including serving multiple English and Japanese voices".
label: core

section: wavenet: long context with no recurrence
text: WaveNet's lesson for text came quickly: ByteNet and ConvS2S translated with convolutions (linked from the Attention Is All You Need page, whose §4 compares their path lengths, O(log k n ) for dilated and O( n / k ) for contiguous filters, with self-attention's O(1)).
label: core

text: Where the lineage ends The transformer (2017) removed the recurrence and kept only attention: self-attention within the encoder and within the decoder, cross-attention from decoder to encoder, so every position is computed at once in training and any two positions are one step apart.
label: core

text: Its paper page animates exactly this contrast, one sentence through a recurrent layer (11 sequential steps) against one self-attention layer (one step), and runs a small trained transformer ( Attention Is All You Need, Reading tab and "Run a Transformer" ).
label: core

text: Two things the RNN gave for free had to be added back: word order, since attention is blind to it ( Positional Encodings ), and a bound on memory per token, since attention keeps every past state (the KV cache).
label: core
key: a bound on memory per token

text: Everything after lives in Topic: llm-architecture , Topic: llm-landscape and Topic: llm-training-and-post-training .
label: core

text: Constant memory and compute per generated token, the RNN's advantage, came back with training that runs in parallel over the sequence: State-space models.
label: core
key: Constant memory and compute per generated token

text: Mamba ( Gu and Dao, December 2023 ) makes the recurrence input-dependent ("selective") and trains it with a parallel scan.
label: depth

text: Its Theorem 1 says the classical gated RNN is a special case of selection; the paper page has a slider for that gate.
label: depth

text: In production the winner is the hybrid: a few attention layers for exact recall, SSM layers for cheap length (Jamba, Nemotron-H, Falcon-H1, on the Mamba page).
label: depth

text: Linear recurrences in RNN form.
label: depth

text: RWKV (2023) and xLSTM (2024, from Hochreiter's group: exponential gating and a matrix memory) scale recurrent language models to billions of parameters; "Were RNNs all we needed?" (2024) strips the LSTM and GRU gates of their dependence on the previous state so they too train with a parallel scan.
label: depth
key: exponential gating and a matrix memory

text: Common mistakes "The LSTM solved vanishing gradients." It gave the gradient one protected path, the cell, scaled only by the forget gate; everything through the hidden state still multiplies Jacobians, and a forget gate below 1 still decays geometrically (0.9 50 ≈ 0.005).
label: depth

text: Untrained, the toy LSTM's gradient 50 steps back is about 10 −6 of its size at the answer (Measured, second view): far better than the plain RNN, nowhere near 1.
label: depth
key: Training opens the path; it does not start open

text: Training opens the path; it does not start open. "A plain RNN cannot remember for long." It can represent a long memory: the toy plain RNN trained on short sequences holds the key for 200 steps.
label: depth
key: A plain RNN cannot remember for long

text: What it cannot do is learn that memory from long sequences, because the gradient that would teach it vanishes first.
label: depth
key: cannot learn that memory from long sequences

text: Representation and learnability are different questions. "The LSTM was introduced with forget, input and output gates in 1997." The forget gate came in 2000 (Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins); the 1997 cell had a fixed self-connection of 1.0.
label: depth

text: See the correction under The LSTM, gate by gate. "king − man + woman = queen." Only once king, man and woman are forbidden as answers; otherwise the nearest word is king.
label: depth
key: Only once king, man and woman are forbidden

text: Without the rule GloVe 50d scores 30.4% on the analogy test instead of 46.2% ( Word vectors ). "Seq2seq always collapses on long sentences." Small, unreversed encoder-decoders did; Sutskever et al.'s deep LSTM with reversed sources "did not suffer on very long sentences".
label: depth
key: 30.4% on the analogy test instead of 46.2%

text: Attention removed the need for such tricks, and with it the fixed-size bottleneck. "Attention was invented by the transformer." It was added to RNN translation in 2014 (Bahdanau et al.) and refined in 2015 (Luong et al.); the transformer's contribution was to remove everything else.
label: depth
key: Attention was invented by the transformer

text: Its paper still describes its dot-product attention against "additive attention", Bahdanau's form. "GRUs are better than LSTMs" (or the reverse).
label: depth

text: Side-by-side studies did not settle it: Chung et al.
label: depth
key: Side-by-side studies did not settle it

text: 2014 could not conclude, Jozefowicz et al.
label: depth

text: 2015 found that "adding a bias of 1 to the LSTM's forget gate closes the gap between the LSTM and the GRU", and Greff et al.
label: depth
key: closes the gap between the LSTM and the GRU

text: 2015 found no variant significantly better than the standard LSTM.
label: depth
key: none significantly better than the standard LSTM

text: The GRU's real advantage is a quarter fewer parameters at the same width. "WaveNet is a recurrent network." It has no recurrence: a stack of dilated causal convolutions, parallel in training.
label: core
key: a quarter fewer parameters at the same width

text: Generation is still one sample at a time because each sample feeds the next, which is why the deployed system was a distilled parallel student.
label: core
key: generation is still one sample at a time

text: Defaults reproduce: the analogy scores (46.2%, 30.4%, 49.7%) are measured here on the released GloVe 6B 50d vectors, independently, with no published 50-dimension figure to compare against; the WaveNet receptive fields (5 for the paper's Figure 2, 1,024 per block of dilations 1 to 512) reproduce the paper independently from the formula; the toy models reproduce Bahdanau et al.'s and Sutskever et al.'s qualitative findings, not their numbers.
label: depth

text: Every number is recomputed by src/recompute.py .
label: depth
key: Every number is recomputed by src/recompute.py
